title: Why Did the Lower Dose Work Better?
subtitle: Bristol Myers Squibb · Phase 3 ALOFT-IPF
text: On Monday, Bristol Myers Squibb shared results from a Phase Three study of admilparant, an experimental medicine for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This condition causes progressive scarring in the lungs, making it harder for patients to breathe. In the trial, people receiving the lower dose showed a smaller decline in lung function over fifty-two weeks than those taking a placebo. But there was a surprise: the higher dose did not reach statistical significance on the study's main measure. The company said the medicine was generally well tolerated in both dose groups. Scientists now want to examine the full data to understand why the results differed. The findings highlight a lesson in drug development: a higher dose does not always lead to a better outcome. Bristol Myers plans to discuss the results with regulators and present more detailed findings at a future medical meeting. For patients, this is encouraging news, but the medicine is still investigational.

choices: Both doses had the same positive result.

modelSummary: Bristol Myers Squibb reported mixed Phase 3 results for an experimental lung disease drug. The lower dose met the trial's main goal, while the higher dose did not reach statistical significance. Researchers need to study the full data before drawing conclusions.
